orchestrator_output.reformulated_query: Administration in early medieval kingdoms Class 8 history
orchestrator_output.text_narration: In early medieval India, new kings took high-sounding titles like Maharaja-adhiraja, meaning 'great king', and Tribhuvana-chakravartin, meaning 'lord of the three worlds'. However, despite these grand titles, kings shared power with subordinates known as Samantas, as well as associations of peasants, traders, and Brahmanas. Resources were collected directly from producers like peasants, cattle-keepers, and artisans, who were often persuaded or compelled to surrender part of their produce. These resources funded the king's establishment, constructed grand temples and forts, and financed wars aimed at expanding trade routes and winning plunder. Positions in revenue collection and administration were often hereditary, passing from father to son within influential families. High administrative posts were frequently given to close relatives of the king or powerful nobles, ensuring loyalty and maintaining central control over the kingdom. Kings rewarded Brahmanas and loyal officers by granting them land, which was recorded on copper plates. These copper plates recorded administrative rights, allowing the grant holder to collect taxes, punish offenders, and manage land resources within the gifted territory.
